title: Applied Econometrics Exercises in R
text:
Preface
This book contains R solutions to exercises from Applied Econometrics by Dimitrios Asteriou and Stephen G. Hall. Each chapter corresponds to a textbook chapter and walks through the data exploration, model building, and interpretation of results.

title: Applied Econometrics Exercises in R
text:
Tools
All exercises are solved using R with the tidyverse ecosystem, including:

tidyverse for data wrangling and visualization
broom for tidy model output
modelsummary for model comparison tables

title: 1  Multiple Regression — Key Ideas
text:
1.1 What is multiple regression?
Simple regression uses one variable to explain another. Multiple regression uses several variables at once. The model looks like:
\[Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 + \ldots + \beta_k X_k + u\]
Each \(\beta\) tells you the effect of that variable holding everything else constant. This is the key insight — you’re isolating individual effects.

title: 1  Multiple Regression — Key Ideas
text:
1.2 Why does it matter?
In the real world, outcomes depend on many things simultaneously. Birth weight depends on both smoking and family income. If you only look at one factor, you might confuse its effect with the effect of something else (omitted variable bias).

title: 1  Multiple Regression — Key Ideas
text:
1.3 Key concepts for the exercises
R² and Adjusted R² — R² tells you what fraction of variation in Y your model explains. But adding any variable increases R², even useless ones. Adjusted R² penalises you for adding variables that don’t help — use it to compare models with different numbers of variables.
F-test (joint significance) — Tests whether all your explanatory variables together are significant. A significant F-test means your model as a whole explains something, even if individual variables might not be.
Wald test — Tests specific hypotheses about coefficients. For example: “Is the effect of smoking exactly twice the effect of income?” You’re testing a restriction on the coefficients.
Adding/removing variables — When you add or drop a variable, the other coefficients change. This happens because variables are correlated with each other. Watch how coefficients shift across your models — it tells you about the relationships between your explanatory variables.

title: 1  Multiple Regression — Key Ideas
text:
1.4 Intuition for Exercise 4.1
You have birth weight, cigarettes smoked, and family income. The question is: does each variable have an independent effect? When you run all three models (both variables, income only, cigarettes only), you’ll see how the estimates change. If a coefficient stays stable across specifications, that variable’s effect is robust. If it swings around, it’s picking up the effect of whatever you left out.

title: 2  Multiple Regression — Questions
text:
Download data for at least 30 stock prices and for the general stock-market index for the stock market of your choice. Using the logarithmic return formula, create the return series for each stock and the market index.
Calculate summary statistics for all stocks and for the market, as well as the correlation matrix of these returns. Comment on your results by referring to mean returns, volatilities, coefficients of skewness and kurtosis, and correlation coefficients.
For each stock, estimate the \(\beta\) coefficient as it is suggested by the CAPM. Summarize and display your results in a table in the text. Comment on the significance of \(\alpha\)s and \(\beta\)s and on the values of \(\beta\)s and \(R^2\)s in terms of what is expected a priori from the theoretical form of the CAPM.
From the results derived in 3, create the required series in order to estimate the SML of the CAPM. Test the relevant hypotheses. Are your results supportive of the CAPM model?
Graph the average returns against the estimated \(\beta\)s (this is a graph of the SML) and comment on your graph with respect to CAPM findings.
Estimate alternative versions with additional variables (such as squared terms of the obtained betas, and the standard deviation of the residuals). Comment on your results.
Compare your findings with those of other empirical studies on this topic.
Write an analytical report of all your analysis. This should include: (a) a short Introduction; (b) a short Literature Review; (c) a Data Set section; (d) an Empirical Results section; and (e) a Conclusions section. Discuss the validity of the CAPM, including references if you refer to any similar studies.

title: 2  Multiple Regression — Questions
text:
2.2 Exercise 4.1
The file health.xls contains data for the following variables:

birth_weight = the weight of infants after birth; when low this can put an infant at risk of illness
cig = number of cigarettes the mother was smoking during pregnancy
fam_inc = the income of the family; the higher the family income the better the access to prenatal care for the family in general

We would expect that the latter two variables affect birth_weight.

Run a regression that includes both variables and explain the signs of the coefficients.
Estimate a regression that includes only fam_inc, and comment on your results.
Estimate a regression that includes only cig and comment on your results.
Present all three regressions summarized in a table and comment on your results, especially by comparing the changes in the estimated effects and the \(R^2\) of the three different models. What does the F-statistic suggest about the joint significance of the explanatory variables in the multiple regression case?
Test the hypothesis that the effect of cig is two times greater than the respective effect of fam_inc, using the Wald test.

Use the data from the file wage.wf1 and estimate an equation that includes as determinants of the logarithm of the wage rate the variables educ, exper and tenure.

Conduct a test of whether another year of general workforce experience (captured by exper) has the same effect on log(wage) as another year of education (captured by educ). title: 4  Multicollinearity — Key Ideas
text:
4.1 What is multicollinearity?
Multicollinearity means your explanatory variables are highly correlated with each other. Imagine trying to figure out whether it’s heat or humidity making you uncomfortable — when both always move together, it’s hard to separate their individual effects.

title: 4  Multicollinearity — Key Ideas
text:
4.2 Why is it a problem?
OLS still works — your estimates are still unbiased. But:

Standard errors blow up — you can’t precisely estimate individual coefficients
t-statistics shrink — variables appear insignificant even when they matter
Coefficients become unstable — small changes in data cause big swings in estimates
Signs may flip — a variable you expect to be positive shows up negative

The model as a whole (F-test, R²) can still look great. The damage is to individual coefficient estimates.

title: 4  Multicollinearity — Key Ideas
text:
4.3 How to detect it

Correlation matrix — high pairwise correlations (above 0.8) are a red flag
VIF (Variance Inflation Factor) — measures how much a coefficient’s variance is inflated. VIF > 10 signals a serious problem
Auxiliary regressions — regress each X on all other Xs. High R² means that X is well-explained by the others (it’s redundant)
Symptom check — high R² but few significant t-stats? Classic multicollinearity sign

title: 4  Multicollinearity — Key Ideas
text:
4.4 What to do about it

Drop one of the collinear variables (if theory permits)
Combine variables (e.g., use a ratio or index)
Get more data (sometimes helps, often doesn’t)
Accept it — if you only care about prediction, not individual coefficients, multicollinearity isn’t really a problem

title: 4  Multicollinearity — Key Ideas
text:
4.5 Intuition for the exercises
In Exercise 5.1, you have GDP and CPI as explanatory variables for imports. Both tend to grow over time — they’re correlated. You’ll see that running separate regressions gives different results than running them together. The auxiliary regression (GDP on CPI) tells you how much of the “blame” goes to multicollinearity vs. genuine insignificance.

title: 7  Heteroskedasticity — Key Ideas
text:
7.1 What is heteroskedasticity?
In a well-behaved regression, the “noise” (error term) has the same spread for all observations — that’s homoskedasticity. When the spread of errors changes systematically (e.g., richer people have more variable spending), that’s heteroskedasticity.
Think of it this way: if you’re predicting house prices, your model might be off by $5,000 for cheap houses but off by $50,000 for expensive ones. The error variance grows with price.

title: 7  Heteroskedasticity — Key Ideas
text:
7.2 Why is it a problem?

OLS estimates are still unbiased — the coefficients are still centred on the truth
But standard errors are wrong — your confidence intervals and t-tests can’t be trusted
You might think a variable is significant when it’s not (or vice versa)

title: 7  Heteroskedasticity — Key Ideas
text:
7.3 How to detect it
Informal:

Plot residuals vs. fitted values — look for a “funnel” or “fan” shape

Formal tests:

White test — general test, doesn’t assume a specific form of heteroskedasticity
Breusch-Pagan test — tests if error variance depends on the explanatory variables
Goldfeld-Quandt test — splits data into two groups and compares variances

title: 7  Heteroskedasticity — Key Ideas
text:
7.4 How to fix it

Robust standard errors (White/HC) — keep OLS but correct the standard errors. Simplest fix and often sufficient
Weighted Least Squares (WLS) — give less weight to observations with higher variance. Requires knowing (or guessing) the form of heteroskedasticity
Log transformation — taking logs of the dependent variable often stabilises variance (because it compresses large values)

title: 7  Heteroskedasticity — Key Ideas
text:
7.5 Intuition for the exercises
In Exercise 6.1, house prices have more variable errors for larger houses (more sqfeet = more variation in price). You’ll test for this, then try fixing it by “weighting down” the noisy observations. Exercise 6.5 shows that simply taking log(price) can eliminate heteroskedasticity — a practical trick used constantly in applied work.

title: 10  Misspecification — Key Ideas
text:
10.1 What is model misspecification?
Your regression assumes a specific relationship between variables. If that assumption is wrong — wrong functional form, missing variables, or irrelevant variables included — your model is misspecified. The estimates may be biased, and your conclusions unreliable.

title: 10  Misspecification — Key Ideas
text:
10.2 Types of misspecification
Wrong functional form — The true relationship is curved but you fitted a straight line. Or it’s logarithmic but you used levels.
Omitted variables — You left out something important that’s correlated with your included variables. This biases your estimates.
Irrelevant variables — You included something that doesn’t belong. This doesn’t bias anything but inflates standard errors (wastes degrees of freedom).

title: 10  Misspecification — Key Ideas
text:
10.3 Functional forms — which to use?








Model
Equation
Interpretation of β




Linear
\(Y = \beta X\)
1-unit increase in X → β-unit change in Y


Log-linear
\(\ln(Y) = \beta X\)
1-unit increase in X → (β×100)% change in Y


Linear-log
\(Y = \beta \ln(X)\)
1% increase in X → β/100 change in Y


Double-log
\(\ln(Y) = \beta \ln(X)\)
1% increase in X → β% change in Y (elasticity)

title: 10  Misspecification — Key Ideas
text:
10.4 Key tools
Ramsey RESET test — Tests whether your model needs nonlinear terms (squared, cubed values of fitted Y). If it rejects, your functional form is likely wrong.
Box-Cox transformation — Helps you choose between linear and log specifications using a data-driven parameter λ. When λ = 1, use linear; when λ → 0, use logs.
Wald/F-tests for restrictions — Test whether higher-order polynomial terms are needed (is the cost function cubic? quadratic? linear?).

title: 10  Misspecification — Key Ideas
text:

title: 13  Dummy Variables — Key Ideas
text:
13.1 What are dummy variables?
Dummy variables turn qualitative categories (male/female, married/single, north/south) into numbers your regression can use. They take the value 1 or 0:
\[\text{male} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if male} \\ 0 & \text{if female} \end{cases}\]

title: 13  Dummy Variables — Key Ideas
section: 13.2 How do they work in regression?
text:
13.2 How do they work in regression?
In the model \(\text{wage} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{male} + u\):

For females: \(E[\text{wage}] = \beta_0\) (the baseline)
For males: \(E[\text{wage}] = \beta_0 + \beta_1\)

So \(\beta_1\) is the difference between the two groups. If \(\beta_1 = 200\), males earn $200 more on average.

title: 13  Dummy Variables — Key Ideas
text:
13.3 The dummy variable trap
If you have 3 categories (north/south/west), you need only 2 dummies. If you include all 3 plus a constant, you get perfect multicollinearity. The excluded category becomes your reference group — all coefficients are measured relative to it.

title: 13  Dummy Variables — Key Ideas
text:
13.4 Interaction effects
You can let a dummy change both the intercept and the slope:
\[Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D + \beta_2 X + \beta_3 (D \times X) + u\]
Here \(\beta_1\) shifts the intercept for group D=1, and \(\beta_3\) changes how X affects Y for that group.

title: 13  Dummy Variables — Key Ideas
text:
13.5 Structural breaks (Chow test)
Does the relationship change before and after an event? Use dummies for time periods and test whether coefficients differ. If they do, you have a “structural break” — one model doesn’t fit both periods.

title: 13  Dummy Variables — Key Ideas
text:
13.6 Intuition for the exercises
Exercise 9.1 asks whether being Black affects wages. First a simple comparison (just the dummy), then adding controls (education, experience). The key insight: the raw wage gap combines discrimination and differences in characteristics. Adding controls isolates the gap that can’t be explained by observable differences. Watch how the dummy coefficient changes as you add variables — that tells you what’s driving the gap.

title: 16  Limited Dependent Variable — Key Ideas
text:
16.1 What’s the problem?
Sometimes your dependent variable is binary — yes/no, approved/denied, pass/fail. Standard OLS doesn’t work well here because:
crumbs: 16  Limited Dependent Variable — Key Ideas

title: 16  Limited Dependent Variable — Key Ideas
text:
It can predict probabilities below 0 or above 1 (nonsense)
The errors can’t be normally distributed when Y is only 0 or 1
The relationship between X and P(Y=1) isn’t linear — it’s S-shaped
crumbs: 16  Limited Dependent Variable — Key Ideas

title: 16  Limited Dependent Variable — Key Ideas
text:
16.2 Three approaches
Linear Probability Model (LPM) — Just run OLS anyway. Simple and often “good enough” for marginal effects, but gives impossible predictions and has heteroskedastic errors by construction.
Probit — Assumes the underlying latent variable has a normal distribution. The probability follows the cumulative normal (Φ):
\[P(Y=1|X) = \Phi(\beta_0 + \beta_1 X)\]
Logit — Uses the logistic function instead. Very similar results to probit in practice:
\[P(Y=1|X) = \frac{e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 X}}{1 + e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 X}}\]
crumbs: 16  Limited Dependent Variable — Key Ideas

title: 16  Limited Dependent Variable — Key Ideas
text:
16.3 Interpreting coefficients
In probit/logit, the raw coefficients don’t directly tell you “a 1-unit increase in X changes the probability by β.” You need marginal effects — the change in probability for a small change in X, evaluated at some point (usually the mean).
crumbs: 16  Limited Dependent Variable — Key Ideas

title: 16  Limited Dependent Variable — Key Ideas
text:
16.4 Key insight
The S-shape means the effect of X on probability depends on where you are. Moving from 10% to 20% probability is different from moving from 45% to 55%, even if the change in X is the same. Effects are largest in the middle and shrink near 0 and 1.
crumbs: 16  Limited Dependent Variable — Key Ideas

title: 16  Limited Dependent Variable — Key Ideas
text:
16.5 Intuition for the exercises
Exercise 12.1 examines loan approval discrimination. You estimate whether being White increases approval probability — first alone, then controlling for financial characteristics. The question is: does the “race effect” shrink or disappear once you account for income, credit history, etc.? If it persists, that’s evidence of discrimination beyond what financial factors explain.
